3. By the previous Orders, this Court has prescribed the
schedule  for  hearings  as  well  as  for  filing  the

## Page 44

3
periodical  Reports  by  the  Supreme  Court  Monitoring
Committee (SCMC). The monitoring and the implementation
of the SWM Rules, 2026, as per the Calendar set out by
the Court, are nearing the halfway mark. The SCMC has
filed  a  48-page  Short-Term  Report,  together  with
Annexures running to 387 pages.
4. The Short-Term Report places before the Court the
percolation  of  the  directions  of  the  Supreme  Court
through the Supreme Court-empowered Monitoring Committee
to the Chief Secretaries of the States, Collectors and
the Local Bodies for compliance.
5. We have carefully examined the Short-Term Report and
the accompanying Annexures.
6. The Supreme Court notes and acknowledges that the
first two phases i.e., kickstarting and putting in place
the  administrative  mechanism  for  monitoring  the
implementation of the SWM Rules, 2026 are in place. The
Report and the Annexures demonstrate that the Supreme
Court’s directions have percolated, in letter and in

## Page 45

4
spirit, through the SCMC to the Chief Secretaries, the
District Collectors and the Heads of Local Bodies. The
SCMC is fully compliant with the timelines stipulated in
this regard. We place on record a few of the achieved
milestones by the SCMC, as under:
a) The SCMC convened four meetings with the constituents
and stakeholders for informing the directions of this
Court.
b) The letter dated 10.09.2026, addressed to the Chief
Secretaries  of  the  States,  the  Railways,  Defence,
Information and Broadcasting and Education Departments,
sets out in categorical terms the targets to be achieved
by the addressees. It is a matter of record that the
directive was followed up with reminders on 06.10.2026,
27.10.2026, 31.10.2026 and 02.11.2026.
c) 755  of  784  District  Collectors  are  on  the  CPCB
Portal. Special Cells exist in 59% of Districts of the
Country.
   

## Page 46

5
d) 4958  out  of  5049  ULBs  and  699  of  701  District
Panchayats are onboarded.
e) The Report refers to convening Special Gram Sabhas in
89102 Gram Panchayats across the country.
f) The  Report  notes  the  installation  of  4592
Interception Systems and the removal of 21324.69 metric
tonnes  of  waste  from  the  banks  and  water  bodies.
Restoration of 778 river stretches is either underway or
substantially  complete.  In  the  centrally  sponsored
programme  “Swachhta  Hi  Seva  2026”,  about  2.1  crore
citizens, out of a total population of 140 crore, across
4861 LBs, are claimed to have participated.
7. The administrative persuasion of the SCMC is clearly
discernible from the above details. The milestones, both
on the Orders of this Court and on the obligations under
the SWM Rules, 2026, are still far from realisation.
8. To wit,  the Report  highlights weaknesses  in the
implementation of the SWM Rules, 2026.

## Page 47

6
9. As many as 400 Districts (approximately) have yet to
formulate and put in place Special Cells to assist the
District Collectors. 9 out of 28 States comply with the
Urban Bylaw target. 16 States do not report on the
incorporation of Rural Bylaws. 18 States do not report
on rural four-way segregation of solid waste, which runs
contrary to the desired performance from Special Cells
in the respective Districts.
10. The targets of the directives and SWM Rules are
already spelt out. The repetition of these directives is
avoided for brevity.
11. This Court, in Municipal Council, Ratlam v. Shri
Vardhichand and others1, a case decided in 1980, when
Bharat was not the economic powerhouse it is today,
declared that Municipalities, i.e., the Local Bodies,
cannot  shirk  their  principal  duty,  i.e.,  health,
hygiene, and habitable conditions, by pleading financial
inability, and declined to accept financial disability
as  a  ground  for  denying  basic  amenities  to  the
1 .  (1980) 4 SCC 162

## Page 48

7
constituents of the Local Bodies. In the last few
decades, Bharat has seen substantial and perceptible
economic growth. Therefore, a plea that failed in 1980
will definitely not work in the third decade of the 21st
Century. To shrug off complacency and simultaneously to
underscore the difference in the country’s standing
between  1980  and  today;  the  following  details  are
referred to. The data is sourced from the websites2.

## Page 49

8
12. The Court notes that Bharat is now a rich country but
has poor sanitation performance. The growth achieved in
other fields is completely negated by the negative impact
from this manageable dereliction by all the stakeholders.
There is a need to emphasise that poor sanitation and
solid waste management affect the outlook of our society
and country. There are instances where similar economies,
within India and outside India, have succeeded in their
sanitation and hygiene objectives. Our existing resources
make  it  possible,  albeit  through  unwavering
implementation by the statutory enforcing authorities and


## Page 50

9
adherence by the citizens.
13. This Court, after reviewing all the Reports filed by
SCMC, observes that each organ of the State has spun on
its own wheel. The cogs (citizens) that connect them must
work towards the objective for realising good result. The
Constitution  embodies  separation  of  powers,  as  basic
structure.  The  Parliament  on  its  turn  enacted  the
Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, and the Executive has
framed the SWM Rules, 2026. Despite the Law and the Rules
in existence, the performance of the SWM Rules, 2016 and
2026, falls short of the objective set by the Parliament.
Therefore,  this  Court,  as  a  repository  of  the
Constitutional  Right  to  a  Pollution-Free  Environment,
through SCMC, has taken the arduous task of issuing
continuing Mandamus to the Local Bodies. This effort of
the Supreme Court through the SCMC is not the fifth wheel
trying to drive the other four wheels. As already noted
in our earlier Orders, it is now or never. The SCMC's
efforts  will  sunset  into  self-regulation  by  the
contributors.

## Page 51

10
14. This Court, drawing on experience and wisdom, and
also conscious of the magnitude of the problem and the
efforts required to address it, has, reposed trust in
SCMC and the District Collectors across the country. The
present set of District Collectors are meritorious and
the successful candidates in the toughest competitive
examination held in the Country. The officers achieve
success through clear strategy, disciplined execution,
and a deep understanding of the syllabus, rather than
mere rote learning or raw hours of study. With the
training the Officers have been provided over years, they
have to revisit all the details that helped them fulfill
their dreams of becoming Administrators and implement the
Court orders to provide the country with a good and
habitable  environment.  The  Court,  with  personal
experience of the perfect and punctilious performance of
two or three District Collectors in the States where such
rules  were  executed  through  District  Collector,  has
relied only on the District Collectors to achieve the
objective of the Court and the rules. The present Order
is not an inspirational quote to the District Collectors
but a reminder of the Apex Court’s expectations in them

## Page 52

11
and their capacity, inasmuch as failure in the on going
affairs will make the situation worse and remediless.
Therefore, the District Collectors reinvent the needed
strategies as per local requirements and, in a dynamic
way,  assist  the  Chief  Secretaries  and  SCMC  in
implementing SWM rules, 2026 the Court Orders.
15. The  Court  notes  the  following  deficiencies  for
action:
I. This Court, vide Order dated 18.08.2026, has noted
that the unorganised residential, commercial and business
sectors form a major part of the problem. The Report is
silent on the notices served and on additional areas
identified  that  warrant  temporary  disconnection  of
water/electricity for due compliance with the SWM Rules,
2026.
II. The public-private participation, an idea floated to
reduce the stress on financial resources, is not spelt
out.

## Page 53

12
III. The  necessary  statutory  framework  for  CSR
initiatives  to  augment  infrastructure  needs  is  not
adverted to.
IV. The SCMC, through the proper framework, mandates
industrial houses to spend CSR fund on solid waste
management infrastructure at the place where the industry
is located. The industries cannot be heard to say that
the pollution  is generated  at a  place and  the CSR
contribution is made elsewhere.
V. The SCMC provides its suggestions to the Court for
further  deliberation  and  for  issuing  necessary
directives.
VI. The Report is silent on biogas and waste-to-energy
plants;  any  other  sustainable  and  renewable  options
explored by the Ministries.
VII.  The method of handling solid waste appears to be
the primary cause of the shortfall in implementing SWM
Rules. The Report is silent on the initiatives undertaken

## Page 54

13
by the State Governments to educate children and make
them volunteers for the implementation of SWM Rules. As
already noted, this is the softest and least coercive way
to effect change in citizens' attitudes towards SWM
Rules. This is an important objective, and the State
Governments  have  not  responded  adequately  despite
reminders dated 06.10.2026 and 30.10.2026 from SCMC.
VIII. The Railways' response is neither positive nor
encouraging. The Railways mapped 630 out of 8809 stations
to  Local  Bodies.  Similarly,  only  510  premises  were
segregated and follow four-way waste handling. The SCMC
issues further directions to the Railways for complete
compliance of SCMC directions within eight weeks from
today.
IX. The Report does not include a reply from the Ministry
of Defence.
X. Similarly, despite SCMC addressing the Registrars
General of the High Courts for due compliance with the
SWM Rules, 2016, neither a status report nor a reply is

## Page 55

14
received from the Registrar Generals of the High Courts.
The only exception is the Lucknow Bench of the Central
Administrative Tribunal. As the Judiciary, we should be
first and foremost in implementing the Fundamental Duty
enshrined in Article 51A(g) of the Constitution of India
and  the  moral  ground  is  added  to  constitutional
jurisdiction conferred on the Judiciary.
XI. The Report does not consolidate details on the waste
generated during the subject period and on how the Local
Bodies account for it.
16. The directions already issued are again examined and
performance audited, and all necessary steps are taken by
the Chief Secretaries and the District Collectors. As a
step forward, the following is directed for necessary
action by the SCMC, to be incorporated in its next
Report:
a) The Chief Secretaries, are directed to instruct all
the  District  Collectors  to  upload  a  geotagged  and
timestamped timeline photograph showing the status of the

## Page 56

15
facilities  in  ULBs  and  RLBs  as  on  21.11.2026.  The
progress and state of the facilities as on 01.01.2027.
b) The SCMC collates the information and, through its
next Report, places a brief status report District wise
on verifiable parameters before this Court.
c) The District Collectors are called upon to report
category-wise,  including  private  establishments,  BWG-
identified establishments, the deficiency noted, and the
steps taken, including notices issued for non-compliance
with SWM Rules, 2026. The present Tech-Savvy District
Collectors  need  not  be  informed  of  the  technical
advancement for virtual inspection and monitoring of SWM
Rules within their jurisdiction.
d) The  District  Collector,  finds  out  through  drone
surveys and video-call inspections, and ascertains the
performance on the ground through the staff of the Local
Bodies.
e) The Education Department of the States is called upon

## Page 57

16
to comply with the earlier Orders without further delay.
17. Paragraph 8 of the Order dated 05.05.2026 reads
as under:  
 
8. “The Secretaries, viz, (i) Secretary,
MoEFCC;  (ii)  Secretary,  Department  of
Drinking Water and Sanitation, Ministry of
Jal Shakti; (iii) Secretary, MoHUA; (iv)
Secretary, Ministry of Panchayati Raj; and
(v)  Secretary,  Ministry  of  Rural
Development, are directed to deliberate
upon  and  explore  the  inclusion  of
contributions  under  Corporate  Social
Responsibility (“CSR”) by industries for
the  establishment  of Compressed  Biogas
plants or such other latest technology as
may be available for converting waste into
energy into the extant scheme and the
modalities for availing the funds. Such
contributions  shall,  to  the  requisite
extent, compensate and follow principles
similar to the Polluter Pays Principle for
the overall upkeep of local bodies. This
is not to strictly enforce the principle
of  the  Polluter  Pays,  but  for  the
amelioration of the environment, CSR funds
shall  be  utilised  exclusively  for  the
improvement of local bodies within whose
jurisdictions the contributing industries
are  located.  We  direct  that  such
contributions be prioritised within the
schemes operated by the Union of India.”
and is implemented in letter and spirit.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NOS.         OF 2026
(Arising out of SLP(C) NOS. 18907-18908/2026)
M/S KALINDI ASSOCIATES                        Appellant(s)
VERSUS
M/S BHARAT COMMERCE AND INDUSTRIES 
LIMITED & ORS.                          Respondent(s)
 O R D E R
Leave granted.
2. Being aggrieved by the order dated 23.04.2026 passed
in Company Appeal No.12 of 2026 as well as the order dated
11.05.2026 passed in Review Petition No.954/2026, by the
Division Bench of the Madhya Pradesh High Court at Indore
the appellant is before this Court.
3. Briefly stated, the facts of the case are that
respondent No.1 herein, namely M/s Bharat Commerce and
Industries  Limited  underwent  liquidation.  Pursuant
thereto, an e-auction was conducted in respect of Plot
Nos. 45-A & B, 47,48, 51, 52, 54 & 55 situated at
Industrial Area, Town No.2, Rajpura, Punjab admeasuring
approximately 2,40,500 sq. ft on 29.01.2025, wherein the
appellant herein, namely M/s Kalindi Associates emerged as
1

## Page 79

the highest bidder with an offer of Rs. 31,00,00,000/-
(Rupees Thirty One Crores only). However, subsequent to
the conclusion of the auction, a third party who was a
stranger to the entire auction process, namely M/s Maa
Sharda  Oils,  submitted  a  higher  offer  of  Rs.
35,00,00,000/- (Rupees Thirty-Five Crores only). When the
Official Liquidator communicated this offer to the High
Court, by order dated 27.09.2025, the High Court rejected
the same but directed the Official Liquidator to inquire
whether the appellant herein would be willing to revise
its bid to Rs. 35,00,00,000/- (Rupees Thirty Five Crores
only). The petitioner herein conveyed its willingness to
enhance its bid to the said amount of Rs.35,00,000/-
(Rupees Thirty-Five Lakhs only). 
4. Respondent No.2 herein, who is also a non-participant
to the auction process, filed an interlocutory application
before the High Court seeking to participate in the
auction process. By a common order dated 16.03.2026, the
learned Single Judge of the High Court rejected the
aforesaid interlocutory application and also accepted the
enhanced  bid  of  the  appellant  of  Rs.  35,00,00,000/-
(Rupees Thirty-Five Crores only). Against this order,
2

## Page 80

respondent No.2 herein preferred Company Appeal No.12/2026
before a Division Bench of the High Court. By order dated
23.04.2026, the Division Bench allowed the appeal and
remanded the earlier-rejected interlocutory application
filed by respondent No.2 to the learned Single Judge for
fresh consideration, and directed the Official Liquidator
to refrain from executing the sale deed in favour of
appellant in the meanwhile. This was on the basis of
certain precedents of this Court which held that even if
the sale certificate had been issued, if there were higher
offers by a third party, then they could be considered.
Against this order, the appellant herein preferred Review
Petition No.954/2026 before the Division Bench of the High
Court. On 11.05.2026, the Division Bench dismissed the
aforesaid review petition on the basis that the earlier
order passed in the company appeal, merely being one of
remand, did not call for any interference.
5. Hence, the instant appeals.
6. We  have  heard  learned  senior  counsel  for  the
appellant and learned senior counsel for respondent No.2
and learned counsel for respondent Nos.1 and 3 (Official
Liquidator representing the Company in Liquidation). We
3

## Page 81

have also perused the material on record.
7. By the impugned order, the High Court remanded to the
learned  Company  Judge,  I.A.  No.170/2026  filed   by
respondent No.2 herein to be heard afresh, while setting
aside the order passed on I.A. No.11913/2025, filed by the
appellant herein,  vide order dated 16.03.2026 by the
learned Company Judge of the Madhya Pradesh High Court at
Indore Bench. 
8. Admittedly, respondent No.2 was not a participant in
the auction proceedings which took place on 29.01.2025.
Admittedly, at that auction conducted on the aforesaid
date, the appellant was the highest bidder and the bid for
a sum of Rs.31 crores was accepted for the subject land
when the reserve price was Rs.29 crores. Later appellant
also enhanced his offer to Rs.35 Crores. However, it is
thereafter that respondent No.2 herein sought to intervene
in the proceedings through filing I.A. No.170/2026 by
contending that he was willing to offer a sum of Rs.42.25
crores. The said application was dismissed by the learned
Single Judge. However, the Division Bench remanded the
matter to the learned Company Judge to reconsider the said
application. 
4

## Page 82

9. We find that the Division Bench was not right in
remanding the matter to the learned Company Judge to
reconsider the application filed by respondent No.2 for
the following reasons: Respondent No.2 is a stranger to
the auction proceedings. We say so for the reason that he
was not a participant in the auction process and in the
actual auction which took place on 29.01.2025. Neither he
did participate in the auction nor did he make any bid on
the said date. Therefore, respondent No.2 is a stranger
and not a person aggrieved by the auction which took place
on the said date in which the appellant was declared to be
the highest bidder. That being the position of respondent
No.2, he could not have intervened in the liquidation
proceedings  by  filing  an  application  namely,  I.A.
No.170/2026. It was highly speculative and without any
locus standi on the part of the said respondent to have
filed the said application at all. 
10. The learned Company Judge, in our view, rightly
declined  to  entertain  the  prayer  of  respondent
No.2/applicant and dismissed the same. The Division Bench
however, has failed to notice the fact that respondent
No.2  herein  who  filed  I.A.  No.170/26  had  no  locus
5

## Page 83

whatsoever to file the said application and the same had
been rightly declined/rejected by the learned Company
Judge. In that view of the matter, we find that the
Division Bench was not right in remanding the matter to
the learned Company Judge to rehear I.A.No.170/2026. 
11. In this context, we wish to rely on the decision of
this Court in the case of  Jasbhai Motibhai Desai vs.
Roshan Kumar, Haji Bashir Ahmed, AIR 1976 SC 578. The
relevant paragraphs read as under:
“33. This Court has laid down in a number of
decisions that in order to have the locus standi
to invoke the extraordinary jurisdiction under
Article 226, an applicant should ordinarily be
one who has a personal or individual right in the
subject-matter of the application, though in the
case of some of the writs like habeas corpus or
quo warranto this rule is relaxed or modified. In
other words, as a general rule, infringement of
some legal right or prejudice to some legal
interest inhering in the petitioner is necessary
to give him a locus standi in the matter…….
xxx
36. It will be seen that in the context of locus
standi to apply for a writ of certiorari, an
applicant may ordinarily fall in any of these
categories:  (i)  “person  aggrieved”;  (ii)
“stranger”;  (iii)  busybody  or  meddlesome
interloper. Persons in the last category are
easily distinguishable from those coming under
the first two categories. Such persons interfere
in  things  which  do  not  concern  them.  They
masquerade as crusaders for justice. They pretend
to act in the name of Pro Bono Publico, though
they have no interest of the public or even of
6

## Page 84

their own to protect. They indulge in the past-
time of meddling with the judicial process either
by force of habit or from improper motives.
Often, they are actuated by a desire to win
notoriety or cheap popularity; while the ulterior
intent of some applicants in this category, may
be  no  more  than  spoking  the  wheels  of
administration. The High Court should do well to
reject the applications of such busybodies at the
threshold.
37. The distinction between the first and second
categories of applicants, though real, is not
always well-demarcated. The first category has,
as it were, two concentric zones; a solid central
zone of certainty, and a grey outer circle of
lessening  certainty  in  a  sliding  centrifugal
scale,  with  an  outermost  nebulous  fringe  of
uncertainty.  Applicants  falling  within  the
central zone are those whose legal rights have
been infringed. Such applicants undoubtedly stand
in the category of “persons aggrieved”. In the
grey outer circle the bounds which separate the
first  category  from  the  second,  intermix,
interfuse  and  overlap  increasingly  in  a
centrifugal direction. All persons in this outer
zone may not be “persons aggrieved”.
38.  To  distinguish  such  applicants  from
“strangers”, among them, some broad tests may be
deduced from the conspectus made above. These
tests  are  not  absolute  and  ultimate.  Their
efficacy varies according to the circumstances of
the case, including the statutory context in
which the matter falls to be considered. These
are: Whether the applicant is a person whose
legal right has been infringed? Has he suffered a
legal wrong or injury, in the sense, that his
interest,  recognised  by  law,  has  been
prejudicially and directly affected by the act or
omission of the authority, complained of? Is he a
person who has suffered a legal grievance, a
person  “against  whom  a  decision  has  been
pronounced which has wrongfully deprived him of
something or wrongfully refused him something, or
7

## Page 85

wrongfully affected his title to something?” Has
he a special and substantial grievance of his own
beyond some grievance or inconvenience suffered
by him in common with the rest of the public? Was
he  entitled  to  object  and  be  heard  by  the
authority before it took the impugned action? If
so, was he prejudicially affected in the exercise
of  that  right  by  the  act  of  usurpation  of
jurisdiction on the part of the authority? Is the
statute, in the context of which the scope of the
words “person aggrieved” is being considered, a
social  welfare  measure  designed  to  lay  down
ethical or professional standards of conduct for
the community? Or is it a statute dealing with
private rights of particular individuals?
xxx
50. The instant case falls well-nigh within the
ratio of this Court's decision in Nagar Rice and
Flour Mills v. N.T. Gowda, (1970) 3 SCR 846 =
(AIR 1971 SC 246) wherein it was held that a rice
mill-owner has no locus standi to challenge under
Article 226, the setting up of a new rice-mill by
another  —  even  if  such  setting  up  be  in
contravention of Section 8(3)(c) of the Rice
Milling Industry (Regulation) Act, 1958 — because
no  right  vested  in  such  an  applicant  is
infringed.”
12. Moreover, we also rely on the recent judgment of this
Court in the cases of Golden Food Products India vs. State
of U.P. and Ors.,    2026 SCC OnLine SC 24   (“Golden Food  
Products India”) and Eva Agro Feeds (P) Ltd. vs. Punjab
National Bank, (2023) 10 SCC 189 (“Eva Agro Feeds (P)
Ltd.”). In Golden Food Products India, this Court observed
in paragraphs 21, 22 and 32 as under:
“21. In K. Kumara Gupta v. Sri Markendaya & Sri
8

## Page 86

Omkareswara Swamy Temple, (2022) 5 SCC 710, it was
observed by this Court that unless and until it
was found that there was any material irregularity
and/or illegality in holding the public auction
and/or the auction was vitiated by any fraud or
collusion, it is not open to set aside the auction
or sale in favour of the highest bidder on the
basis of some representation made by a third party
who did not even participate even in the auction
proceedings and did not make any offer. If there
is repeated interference in the auction process,
the object and purpose of holding public auction
and its sanctity would be frustrated. That unless
there are allegations of fraud, collusion, etc.,
the highest offer received in the public offer
should be accepted as a fair value. Otherwise,
there shall not be any sanctity of any public
auction.
22. In Eva Agro Feeds, it was observed that the
mere expectation of the liquidator (in the said
case) which could also mean the auction seller
that, a still higher price may be obtained can be
no  good  ground  to  cancel  an  otherwise  valid
auction and go in for another round of auction.
Such a course of action would not only lead to
incurring of avoidable expenses but also erode
credibility of the auction process itself. Thus,
the auctioning authority must adhere to the rule
of  law  and  an  auction  cannot  be  cancelled
arbitrarily.
xxx
32. An auction process has a sanctity attached to
it and only for valid reasons that the highest bid
can be discarded in an auction which is otherwise
held in accordance with law. If a valid bid has
been made which is above the reserve price, there
should be a rationale or reason for not accepting
it. Therefore, the decision to discard the highest
bid must have a nexus to the rationale or the
reason. Merely because the authority conducting
the auction expected a higher bid than what the
highest bidder had bid cannot be a reason to
discard the highest bid….”
9

## Page 87

13. In Eva Agro Feeds (P) Ltd., this Court in paragraph
71 observed as under:
“71.  A  conjoint  reading  of  the  aforesaid
provisions would make it clear that while the
highest bidder has no indefeasible right to demand
acceptance of his bid, the Liquidator if he does
not want to accept the bid of the highest bidder
has to apply his mind to the relevant factors.
Such  application  of  mind  must  be  visible  or
manifest in the rejection order itself. As this
Court has emphasised the importance and necessity
of  furnishing  reasons  while  taking  a  decision
affecting  the  rights  of  parties,  it  is
incomprehensible that an administrative authority
can take a decision without disclosing the reasons
for taking such a decision.”
14. Merely because a person who has not participated in
an auction proceedings and is a stranger thereto seeks to
enter the fray by making a higher bid at a later stage
would not confer any locus or right on such a party to
seek conferment of the bid in his favour. 
15. In the circumstances, we set aside the impugned order
of the Division Bench of the High Court. We also dismiss
I.A. No.170/2026 filed by respondent No.2 herein. The
appeals are allowed in the aforesaid terms.
16. No costs.
17. At this stage, learned senior counsel categorically
10

## Page 88

submitted that the appellant has already deposited a sum
of Rs.35 crores and the said fact is also acknowledged by
learned counsel for the Official Liquidator.
18. The official liquidator shall handover possession of
the subject land to the appellant herein immediately after
all legal formalities are completed including registration
of the sale deed.
19. All  pending  applications  including  intervention
application shall stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.        OF 2026
(Arising out of SLP (Criminal) No. 9897 of 2026)
SARASWATHI     APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
ROHITH KUMAR ALIAS REVANNA & ANR.    RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The present appeal arises out of the impugned
order dated 30.04.2025 passed by the High Court of
Judicature at Madras in Crl. O.P. No. 11432 of 2025,
whereby the High Court allowed the petition preferred
by respondent No. 1 (accused) and set aside the order
dated 01.04.2025 passed by the District Munsif-cum-
Judicial Magistrate No. 1, Hosur in Crl. M.P. No. 224
of 2025, cancelling his bail.
3. The factual matrix of the case, as emerging from
the record, is that an FIR bearing Crime No. 278 of
2024 was registered on the complaint of the Village
Administrative Officer upon recovery of the dead body
1

## Page 123

of the deceased (a 22-year-old law student) on a public
road. Investigation revealed that respondent No. 1,
owing to previous enmity, along with other co-accused
persons, abducted the deceased and attacked him with
lethal weapons, causing his death. Respondent No. 1 was
arrested on 08.10.2024 and was subsequently released on
default bail under Section 167(2) of the Code of
Criminal Procedure, 1973, on 07.01.2025, after having
remained in custody for approximately three months.
4. Thereafter, on 09.01.2025, another criminal case
bearing Crime No. 12 of 2025 was registered against
respondent No. 1 and other co-accused persons when they
were intercepted travelling in two cars in a rash and
negligent manner and were found in possession of five
pistols. Respondent No. 1 was arrested and remained in
custody until he was granted bail in Crime No. 12 of
2025 on 12.03.2025 in Criminal M.P. No. 675 of 2025 by
the  District  and  Sessions  Court,  Krishnagiri.
Meanwhile, during the course of investigation in Crime
No. 278 of 2024, respondent No. 1 also extended death
threats to a person who had come to collect the vehicle
involved in the crime. Consequently, an application
seeking cancellation of bail (Criminal M.P. No. 224 of
2

## Page 124

2025) was moved before the District Munsif-cum-Judicial
Magistrate, who, vide order dated 01.04.2025, cancelled
the  bail  granted  to  respondent  No.  1.  Aggrieved
thereby, respondent No. 1 approached the High Court of
Judicature at Madras in Criminal O.P. No. 11432 of
2025, which was allowed vide the impugned order dated
30.04.2025, thereby enlarging respondent No. 1 on bail.
5. Learned counsel appearing for the appellant-
complainant has vehemently argued that respondent No. 1
is a hardcore criminal having a checkered history of
more than 10 criminal cases, including three murder
cases, and that even after his release on bail, fresh
criminal cases were registered against him. Attention
of this Court has also been drawn to the order dated
26.05.2026  passed  by  the  Principal  District  and
Sessions Judge, Bengaluru Rural District, Bengaluru, in
Criminal Miscellaneous No. 395 of 2026, rejecting the
prayer of respondent No. 1 for anticipatory bail in a
subsequent case. It is submitted that respondent No. 1
is the prime accused and main conspirator who abducted
and murdered a 22-year-old law student who used to
assist  illiterate  farmers  in  lodging  complaints
regarding fraud and land grabbing.
3

## Page 125

6. Learned counsel appearing for the State of Tamil
Nadu has supported the submissions advanced on behalf
of the appellant, stating that respondent No. 1 has a
long list of criminal antecedents and has gone to the
extent of threatening prosecution witnesses.
7. On  the  other  hand,  learned  Senior  counsel
appearing for respondent No. 1 (Rohith Kumar Alias
Revanna) has contended that the present appeal has
become  infructuous  inasmuch  as,  subsequent  to  the
transfer  of  investigation,  the  bail  granted  to
respondent  No.  1  was  cancelled  by  the  court  in
Karnataka and the said cancellation order has been
affirmed by the High Court of Karnataka, against which
respondent No. 1 proposes to file a Special Leave
Petition.
8. It is further submitted that respondent No. 1
has been acquitted in three murder cases, though the
long  list  of  other  criminal  antecedents  is  not
disputed. Learned Senior counsel has also raised a
preliminary objection that the matter ought to have
been argued by the Standing Counsel for the State of
Karnataka rather than the State of Tamil Nadu.
9. Heard learned counsel for the parties at length
4

## Page 126

and perused the record. 
10. This Court is of the considered opinion that the
present appeal has certainly not become infructuous, as
this Court is required to scrutinize the legality and
propriety of the impugned order passed by the High
Court  of  Judicature  at  Madras  in  the  facts  and
circumstances of the case.
11. The  appellant  before  this  Court  is  the
unfortunate mother of the deceased,-a lady who has lost
her 22-year-old son, a law student who was fighting for
the downtrodden sections of society, and whose tears
are still flowing on account of the loss of her young
son.
12. Upon  careful  perusal  of  the  record,  it  is
evident that respondent No. 1 remained in custody in
the present case only from 08.10.2024 to 07.01.2025
(about three months) prior to grant of default bail,
and  thereafter  from  09.01.2025  to  12.03.2025  and
01.04.2025 to 30.04.2025. It is indeed unfortunate that
the High Court of Judicature at Madras, while dealing
with the order dated 01.04.2025 cancelling the bail
granted to respondent No. 1, has not at all referred to
or considered the checkered history of criminal cases
5

## Page 127

against respondent No. 1, as well as his subsequent
conduct of threatening witnesses and involvement in
fresh offences while on bail, and has mechanically set
aside the well-reasoned cancellation order passed by
the District Munsif-cum-Judicial Magistrate.
13. Having carefully considered the impugned order
passed by the High Court, keeping in view the brief
period of custody undergone, the gravity and heinous
nature  of  the  offence,  the  extensive  criminal
antecedents of respondent No. 1, and the complete non-
consideration thereof by the High Court, this Court is
of the considered opinion that the impugned order dated
30.04.2025 passed by the High Court of Judicature at
Madras cannot be sustained and deserves to be set
aside.
14. Accordingly,  the  appeal  is  allowed  and  the
impugned order dated 30.04.2025 passed by the High
Court of Judicature at Madras in Criminal O.P. No.
11432 of 2025 is hereby set aside. Consequently, the
order dated 01.04.2025 passed by the District Munsif-
cum-Judicial  Magistrate  cancelling  the  bail  of
respondent No. 1 stands restored.
15. The appeal is allowed in the above terms.
6

disposed of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Having heard the learned senior counsels appearing for the
parties,  we  notice  that  under  Rule  5(6)(b)  of  the  Wetlands
(Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017, a Grievance Committee
8

## Page 139

consisting of four Members would be required to hear and forward
the  grievances  raised  by  the  public  to  the  State  Wetland
Authorities. It is stated in many a cases that the wetland which
has been protected by the orders of this Court, are still being
encroached. It is in this background, we direct the respective
State Governments to constitute a Grievance Committee in compliance
of the aforesaid Rule forthwith if not already constituted. On the
said Committee being constituted, it is needless to state that it
would  commence  effectively  discharging  the  functions  as
contemplated under the Rule and take steps accordingly.
2. Let a copy of this order be circulated to all the Chief
Secretaries of the States for being implemented forthwith.
3. Mr. Shekhar Naphade, learned senior counsel, has circulated a
tentative summary note relating to the steps to be taken for
identifying the wetlands. At this stage, we are of the view that
the  learned  counsels  appearing  for  the  parties  can  have  a
conference in this regard and outline the proposed summary so as to
enable this Court to direct a uniform policy being adopted by all
the States subject to certain variations, if any, depending upon
the geographical status of the States. The tentative note shall be
submitted within an outer limit of two weeks from today.
I.A. No.246847/2026 
1. Application is allowed. Permission is granted to transpose the
applicant as Petitioner No.2 in place of Respondent No.37.
2. Cause title be amended accordingly.
Re-list the matters on 02.12.2026 at 02:00 pm.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Criminal Appeal No(s).    /2026
@SLP (Crl.) No(s).  19631/2026
RAJU KUMAR SINGH                                   Appellant (s)
                                
VERSUS
THE STATE (NCT OF DELHI)                           Respondent(s)
O R D E R
 
1.  Leave granted.
2.  Heard learned counsel for the parties.
3. This appeal impugns the order of the High
Court  of  Delhi  at  New  Delhi,  dated
29.09.2026,  whereby  the  appellant’s
application for suspending his conviction
under Section 304 Part II of the Indian
Penal  Code,  1860  (for  short  ‘IPC’)  and
Section 30 of the Arms Act, 1959 has been
rejected.
4. Prima facie, a celebratory fire while a
dance party was going on resulted in death
1

## Page 141

of a lady. The prosecution evidence, prima
facie, indicated that two persons including
the  appellant  had  indulged  in  making
celebratory shots in the air. One had a .315
bore rifle whereas the appellant had a .22
bore licensed pistol. The deceased, who was
on the dance floor, suffered pellet injuries
on her head resulting in skull fracture,
brain damage and consequent death.
5. Though nobody witnessed the appellant
firing shot at the deceased, the Trial Court
convicted the appellant under Section 304
Part II of IPC by taking into consideration
various  circumstances  and  accordingly
sentenced him to 4 years R.I. The appellant
was also convicted under Section 30 of the
Arms Act for violating terms of arms license
and sentenced to two months thereunder.
6. The sentence part has been stayed by the
High Court, and the appellant is on bail
pending consideration of his appeal by the
High Court. However, being a sitting Member
of Legislative Assembly, the appellant also
2

## Page 142

applied for stay of his conviction to avoid
automatic  disqualification  under  Section
8(3) of the Representation of the People
Act,  1951  (for  short,  R.P.  Act).  This
application  came  to  be  rejected  by  the
impugned order.
7. The argument on behalf of the appellant
is  two-fold.  First,  the  nature  of  the
evidence on record does not make out a case
of culpable homicide not amounting to murder
punishable  under  Section  304  Part  II.
Second, if the prayer for suspension of
conviction is not accepted, the consequences
shall be draconian resulting in loss of
membership in the Legislative Assembly. In
such  an  event,  even  if  the  appeal  is
ultimately  allowed,  the  loss  would  be
irreparable.
8. On the merits of his conviction under
Section 304 Part II of IPC, the submission
on behalf of the appellant is that the
evidence does not at all indicate that the
fire made by the appellant was either aimed
3

## Page 143

at the victim or was so reckless that a
person in the vicinity was likely to be hit
by the fire. It is submitted that the bullet
fragments recovered during autopsy indicate
that the bullet had ricochet from some hard
surface and then entered the skull of the
victim. It is submitted that an offence
punishable under Section 304 Part II of IPC
would  have  to  satisfy  the  following
ingredients i.e. that the act was done with
knowledge that it is likely to cause death,
but without intention to cause death, or
done to cause such bodily injury as is
likely to cause death. In the present case,
it is submitted, the said ingredients are
not satisfied inasmuch as if the bullet
ricochets from some hard substance and then
strikes a person, the act is neither done
with knowledge that it is likely to cause
death nor there is intention to cause such
bodily injury as is likely to cause death.
Hence, conviction under Section 304 Part II
of IPC is,  prima facie, not sustainable.
4

## Page 144

Besides, the evidence on record is sketchy
and  the  conviction  is  based  more  on
inference from the circumstances narrated by
the witnesses than any clinching evidence
against  the  appellant.  According  to  the
learned counsel for the appellant, on the
given set of facts, the appellant cannot be
convicted for an offence graver than one
punishable under Section 304-A of IPC.
9. The  learned  Solicitor  General,  who
appeared for the State, submits that the
arguments  advanced  on  behalf  of  the
appellant would have to be considered and
tested by the High Court against the weight
of  evidence  while  deciding  the  appeal;
therefore, at this stage, no assessment on
merits  be  made.  He,  however,  does  not
dispute the fact that the appellant is a
sitting Member of Legislative Assembly and
if his conviction under Section 304 Part II
of  IPC  is  not  suspended  pending
consideration of his appeal by the High
Court, he would incur disqualification.
5

## Page 145

10.  We have accorded due consideration
to the submissions made before us and have
perused the impugned order as well as the
conviction order passed by the Trial Court.
11. Prima facie, there appears no evidence
to indicate that the gun shot which hit the
victim was fired directly at the victim by
the appellant from the weapon held by him.
Further,  it  appears,  only  fragments  or
particles of bullet were recovered at the
time of autopsy which is suggestive of the
fact that the shot did not directly strike
the  victim;  rather,  prima  facie, the
bullet / fragments of the bullet hit the
victim  after  ricocheting  from  some  hard
surface.  In  such  circumstances,  whether
conviction of the appellant under Section
304 Part II of IPC is sustainable or not, is
a debatable issue which would have to be
thrashed out by the appellate court while
deciding the appeal.
12. Besides, disqualification under Section
8(3) of the R.P. Act occurs when a person is
6

## Page 146

convicted of any offence, other than one
specified in sub-section (1) or sub-section
(2)  of  Section  8,  and  sentenced  to
imprisonment for not less than two years.
Neither the offence punishable under Section
304  Part  II  of  IPC  nor  the  offence
punishable under Section 30 of the Arms Act
fall in any of the categories of offences
specified in sub-section (1) or sub-section
(2) of Section 8 of the R.P. Act and, most
importantly, there is no minimum sentence
prescribed for an offence punishable under
Section 304 Part II.
13.  In such circumstances, having regard
to the facts of the present case, we are of
the view that a case has been made out for
staying  the  conviction  of  the  appellant
under Section 304 Part II of IPC pending
consideration of his appeal by the High
Court.
14.  Consequently, this appeal is partly
allowed. The conviction of the appellant for
the offence punishable under Section 304
7

## Page 147

Part  II  of  IPC  shall  remain  suspended
/stayed pending consideration of his appeal
by the High Court.
15. Pending application(s), if any, shall
stand disposed of.
…………………………………………..J
[MANOJ MISRA]
…………………………………………..J
[VIJAY BISHNOI]
New Delhi;
November 16, 2026

                             O R D E R
Heard learned counsel for the parties. 
2. Mr. S.D. Sanjay, learned Senior Counsel/Convenor and
Coordinator  in  the  present  case  submits  that  general
consultations with the stakeholders were held in Bhopal
through hybrid mode and the South Zone consultation was
held on 4th and 5th September, 2026 in Karnataka Judicial
Academy, Bengaluru. He submits that the next conference is
5

## Page 154

SLP (CRL.) NO.14087/2025
going to be held in Judicial Academy, at Lucknow on 19th and
20th December, 2026. He informs that after this, four zones,
namely, Eastern, Western, Northern and North Eastern would
have to be covered.
3. At  this  juncture,  we  request  Mr.  S.D.  Sanjay  to
explore the feasibility of convening at least one more
conference on 21st and 22nd November, 2026: 
(A) Preferably  of  the  Western  Zone  at  the  Judicial
Academy, High Court of Bombay or the Judicial Academy, High
Court of Rajasthan at Jodhpur or the Judicial Academy, High
Court  of  Gujarat  at  Gandhi  Nagar/Ahmedabad.  All  the
concerned States shall fully cooperate with the learned
Convenor and Coordinator.
OR
(B) Of the Northern Zone, for which the venue may be
decided in consultation with the concerned States/U.Ts,
preferably the Judicial Academy of that State. All the
concerned  States  shall  fully  cooperate  with  Mr.  S.D.
Sanjay, Convenor and Coordinator. 
4. To  ensure  that  there  are  no  last-minute
hiccups/glitches, we direct that all the stakeholders,
especially the concerned States shall ensure that all
logistic infrastructure shall be worked out at least ten
days in advance in terms of whatever would be required by
Mr.  S.D.  Sanjay,  Convenor  and  Coordinator.  The  Chief
6

## Page 155

SLP (CRL.) NO.14087/2025
Secretary, Home Secretary and the Director General of
Police  of  the  concerned  States/U.Ts  shall  personally
monitor and ensure that the said Zonal Conference is held
smoothly.
5. The expenses borne would be equally divided among the
States/U.Ts for which the same is held.
6. Let the Minutes of the Zonal Conferences, as and when
they are held, be filed before this Court within two weeks
from holding of the said meetings. With regard to the Zonal
Conferences held at Bhopal and Bengaluru, the Minutes be
brought on record within two weeks from today.
7. The matter be listed on 01.12.2026 at 3.00 p.m.
8. After  the  order  was  dictated,  Mr.  Vishal  Sinha,
learned counsel who has appeared for the applicant in I.A.
No.278783/2026 draws the attention of the Court to the fact
that because the applicant has raised certain objections
against  certain  persons  who  were  supported  by  local
administration/Police, cases have been fastened on the
applicant one after the other and notice has been issued
against the applicant as to why he may not be externed from
the District concerned.
9. Mr. Pashupathi Nath Razdan, learned Counsel for the
State of Madhya Pradesh submits that this Court may take
notice of the averments made and the issues raised by the
applicant which clearly indicates that it is a deliberate
7

## Page 156

SLP (CRL.) NO.14087/2025
attempt to vitiate social harmony.
10. Having gone through the pleadings in the Interlocutory
Application, we refrain from commenting on the same for the
present. However, the matter is serious and the Court takes
judicial note of the same.
11. Thus,  the  Commissioner  of  Police,  Indore,  is  at
liberty to initiate appropriate action in the matter as he
may deem fit.
12. Any issue arising as a result of action being taken
against  the  applicant  by  the  Commissioner  of  Police,
Indore, which is connected with the issue which has been
raised in the Interlocutory Application, shall not be
entertained by any Court, except this Court in the present
proceedings.
13. We are confident that the Commissioner of Police,
Indore, shall take appropriate action to ensure that under
no circumstances the social fabric of this Country or
communal harmony is disturbed in any manner whatsoever.
14. Before parting, on an issue raised by Mr. S.D. Sanjay,
Convenor and Coordinator, with regard to the conference to
be held on 19th and 20th December, 2026, we direct that all
authorities concerned shall fully cooperate with him to
ensure that the said Conference is held not only on the
said dates, but with full preparedness and in terms of
whatever  is  required  and  conveyed  to  the  concerned
8

## Page 157

SLP (CRL.) NO.14087/2025
States/U.Ts. as also the Union Home Ministry with regard to
the same. All preparations must be made well in advance to
prevent any confusion. The same goes with regard to holding
of  all  conferences/Zonal  Conferences,  including  that
proposed at Lucknow on 19th and 20th December, 2026.

examined by the Committee.

1. Leave granted. 
2. Heard learned counsel for the parties.
3. This appeal arises from an order dated
03.02.2026  passed  by  the  High  Court  of
Madhya  Pradesh  at  Indore  rejecting  the
anticipatory bail prayer of the appellant in
connection  with  Crime  No.  476/2024,
registered  at  Police  Station  Industrial
Area, Jaora, District Ratlam (M.P.)
4. After hearing the learned Counsel for
the appellant, on 27.04.2026 we had passed
an interim order, which is reproduced below:

## Page 176

“1. The learned counsel for
the petitioner is permitted to
implead  the  complainant  as
respondent.
2. Issue notice, returnable in
four weeks.
3. Notice on behalf of the
respondent has been accepted
by Ms. Ritika Singhal, AOR.
4.  In  the  meantime,  it  is
directed  that  if  the
petitioner  is  arrested  in
connection  with  Crime  No.
476/2024, registered at Police
Station  Industrial  Area,
Jaora, District Ratlam (M.P.),
he  shall  be  released  on  a
personal bond of Rs. 25,000/-
subject to an undertaking that
he  shall  cooperate  in  the
investigation and make himself
available for interrogation as
and  when  required  by  the
investigating agency. He shall
also  submit  an  undertaking
that he will not threaten the
witnesses  or  tamper  the
evidence.”

## Page 177

5. After service of notice, the State is
represented.
6. Upon consideration of submissions, we
do not find a good reason to discharge the
interim protection order granted earlier.
7. This appeal is, accordingly, disposed
of  by  making  the  interim  order  absolute
subject to the following conditions:
(A)Within  three  weeks  from  today,  the
appellant shall submit bail bonds to the
satisfaction of the Trial Court along
with an undertaking that he shall co-
operate in the trial/investigation; and 
(B)He  shall  submit  an  additional
undertaking that he will not threaten
the witnesses or tamper the evidence.
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall
stand disposed of.

1. Leave granted.
2. From  the  material  on  record,  it
appears that as against the decree passed by the
Trial Court in appellants’ predecessor’s favour
on  01.09.1986,  the  First  Appellate  Court
reversed  the  decree,  against  which  the
appellants’  predecessor(s)  had  preferred  a
Second Appeal before the High Court in the year
1988, which was admitted for hearing on merits
on 14.07.1988.
3. When the Second Appeal came up for
hearing, the original appellant before the High
Court,  Naranjan Singh, had passed away, and
learned counsel appearing for the appellants
pleaded  no  instructions.  This  resulted  in
dismissal of the Second Appeal for want of

## Page 228

2
prosecution, however, the said development was
not known to the appellants. An application for
restoration of the Regular Second Appeal was
moved  along  with  the  application  seeking
condonation of delay in filing such restoration
application, which has now been rejected by the
Trial Court under the impugned order.
4. Upon hearing learned counsel for the
parties, we are of the considered view that the
delay seems to be occasioned firstly; because of
the mistake of the counsel appearing for the
appellants and thereafter, due to the appellants
being not aware of the dismissal of the Second
Appeal. Moreover, the counsel appearing for the
appellants  in  the  High  Court  pleaded  no
instructions when the Regular Second Appeal came
up for hearing and had no knowledge about the
death of Naranjan Singh.
5. In view of the above, we set aside the
impugned order passed by the High Court and
allow  appellants’  prayer  for  restoration  of
Regular Second Appeal No. 3113 of 1987 for
hearing the same on its own merits.
6. The appeal is accordingly, allowed.

1.  Leave granted.
2. We have heard learned counsel for the parties.
3. Appellant is aggrieved by order dated 22.05.2026,
passed by the High Court of Madhya Pradesh at Jabalpur
(briefly the ‘High Court’ hereinafter) rejecting the
application of the appellant for grant of anticipatory
bail.
4. Appellant has been named as an accused in Crime No.
901 of 2018, registered at Police Station Motinagar,
District Sagar, under Sections 294 and 307/34 of the
Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short, ‘IPC’) read with
1

## Page 248

Sections 25 and 27 of the Arms Act, 1957.
5. As per the prosecution case, complainant Dushyant
Singh alleged that he received firearm injuries at the
hands of the appellant. Appellant is the father of the
deceased-wife of the informant who died an unnatural
death.
6. This Court by order dated 16.07.2026 directed the
Superintendent of Police, Sagar, to file an affidavit
detailing  all  circumstances  of  the  case.  In  the
meanwhile,  interim  protection  was  granted  to  the
appellant subject to the appellant co-operating with the
investigation.
7. In terms of the aforesaid order, respondent-State
of Madhya Pradesh has filed counter affidavit. Respondent
No.2 (informant) has also filed counter affidavit.
8. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that
there is belated registration of the FIR (4 days delay).
This is clearly an after thought by the informant to
implicate the appellant who is the unfortunate father of
the deceased-wife of the informant. His daughter had died
under suspicious and unnatural circumstances within 7
years of marriage for which appellant had lodged FIR
against the informant under Sections 304(B), 498A and 34
IPC read with Sections 3 and 4 of the Dowry Prohibition
Act, 1961. He further submits that pursuant to the
interim protection granted by this Court, appellant has
cooperated with the investigation.
2

## Page 249

9. Learned State counsel submits that while it is true
that there was delay in registration of the FIR for which
notice has been issued to 3 of the erring policemen, the
fact remains that appellant was also responsible for
delay in the investigation. However, after the interim
protection was granted by this Court, appellant appeared
before the Investigating Officer (IO) and has cooperated
with the investigation. Now investigation is complete,
though, chargesheet has not been filed.
10.  Mr. Nachiketa Joshi, learned senior counsel for
the second respondent submits that respondent No.2 had
suffered  a  murderous  assault  at  the  hands  of  the
appellant who had used firearm in the incident. However,
he also acknowledges the bitterness and hostility between
the parties arising out of the unfortunate death of his
wife. Contention of Mr. Nachiketa Joshi is that appellant
did not cooperate with the investigation for a long time
from the year 2019 onwards.
11.  In response, learned counsel for the appellant
submits that it is not correct that appellant did not
cooperate with the investigation.
12.  Submissions  made  by  learned  counsel  for  the
parties have received the due consideration of the Court.
13.  Having regard to the circumstances surrounding the
incident and the statement made by learned State counsel
that following the interim protection granted by this
Court,  the  appellant  had  cooperated  with  the
3

3. While quashing the impugned POA, the Bombay High Court preferred to
1 impugned judgment
2 Bombay High Court
1

## Page 268

agree  with  the  views  expressed  by  a  Division  Bench  of  the  High  Court  at
Calcutta3 in Directorate of Enforcement & Ors. Vs. Union of India & Ors.4;
in the process, however, it disagreed with the opinion expressed by a Division
Bench of the High Court of Delhi at New Delhi5 in Directorate of Enforcement
& Anr. Vs. Vikas WSP Ltd. & Ors.6.
4. The issue that arose for consideration before the Bombay High Court, the
Calcutta High Court and the Delhi High Court happened to be common: whether
extension of the period of limitation ordered by this Court due to COVID related
complications  vide the  order  dated  10th January,  2022  in  Miscellaneous
Application No.21 of 2022 in Suo Moto Writ Petition (C) No.3 of 2020 (titled “In
Re: Cognizance for Extension of Limitation Vs. XXXX”) would save POAs from
lapsing after its validity period of six months. The view of the Calcutta High
Court,  with  which  the  Bombay  High  Court  has  agreed  in  the  impugned
judgment, was that the said order of 10th January, 2022 covered judicial and
quasi-judicial  proceedings  that  aggrieved  parties  could  not  institute  due  to
COVID related restrictions and this Court came to their rescue by extending the
period  of  limitation;  however,  similar  benefit  was  not  extended  to  the
Enforcement Directorate despite an application made by it in that behalf. The
view of the Delhi High Court was, of course, otherwise.
5.  Since  the  Enforcement  Directorate  was  a  common  party  in  both  the
proceedings before the Calcutta and the Delhi High Courts, it would reasonably
be expected that the Calcutta High Court view, being a prior view (2022), ought
to have been placed before the Delhi High Court while it was hearing a similar
issue in 2025. Unfortunately, however, the attention of the Delhi High Court was
3 Calcutta High Court
4 2022 SCC OnLine Cal 3959
5 Delhi High Court
6 2025 SCC OnLine Del 6163
2

## Page 269

not  drawn  by  the  Enforcement  Directorate  to  the  view  expressed  by  the
Calcutta High Court earlier. We wonder, whether the Delhi High Court would
have taken a different view had the decision of the Calcutta High Court been
referred to it.  
6. Be that as it may, the Bombay High Court in the impugned judgment has
recorded that the Enforcement Directorate did not challenge the decision of the
Calcutta High Court. 
7. We  had  posed  a  specific  query  to  Mr.  Suryaprakash  V.  Raju,  learned
Additional  Solicitor  General,  as  to  whether  the  Enforcement  Directorate
challenged the decision of the Calcutta High Court before this Court or not.
While, initially, no direct answer was forthcoming, we were referred to an order
dated 8th May, 2023 passed by a coordinate Bench of this Court in SLP (C) Diary
No. 13081 of 2023 (Directorate of Enforcement & Ors. Vs. Union of India & Ors.)
in course of hearing. 
8. It appears on a reading thereof that the decision of the Calcutta High
Court was, indeed, challenged by the Enforcement Directorate but ultimately, in
light  of  the  final  adjudication  order  having  been  passed,  the  special  leave
petition was withdrawn leaving all questions of law open.
9. Mr. Raju has next placed before us an order dated 16th September, 2026
passed by a co-ordinate Bench of this Court, while dismissing Special Leave
Petition (Crl.) No.16024/2025 (Purushottam Dev Arya & Anr. Vs. Union of India &
Ors.). According to him, with such dismissal, the decision of the Delhi High Court
has been affirmed.
10. Having perused the said order, we find that the same hardly advances the
case of the Enforcement Directorate. The coordinate Bench noted the issue
involved but decided no point except recording its disinclination to interfere.
3

## Page 270

11. Turning to the merits, we are fully convinced that the well-considered,
well-written and well-reasoned impugned judgment of the Bombay High Court
does not require any interference in light of the order dated 10th January, 2022
passed by this Court. 
12. The order dated 10th January, 2022 passed by this Court inter alia directs
that  “the period from 15.03.2020 till 28.02.2022 shall stand excluded for the
purposes of limitation as may be prescribed under any general or special laws
in respect of all judicial or quasi judicial proceedings”. Sub-paragraph (IV) of
paragraph 5 also records that:
“IV. It is further clarified that the period from 15.03.2020 till 28.02.2022 shall
also stand excluded in computing the periods prescribed under Sections 23(4)
and  29A  of  the  Arbitration  and  Conciliation  Act,  1996,  Section  12A  of  the
Commercial Courts Act, 2015 and provisos (b) and (c) of Section 138 of the
Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 and any other laws, which prescribe period(s)
of limitation for instituting proceedings, outer limits (within which the court or
tribunal can condone delay) and termination of proceedings.”
13. The  impugned  judgment  correctly  records  in  paragraph  41  that  sub-
paragraph (IV) (extracted supra) does not include provisions of the Prevention of
Money Laundering Act, 20027 and, in the following paragraph, it also records
that the said order of this Court does not govern PMLA timelines. In fact, the
Bombay  High  Court  clearly  noted  that  this  Court  passed  no  order  on  the
Enforcement Directorate’s application (Interlocutory Application No.91204/2020)
seeking benefit of extension of time due to COVID. Mr. Raju did not dispute such
finding.
14. In our further considered view, the Bombay High Court in the impugned
judgment has correctly applied the law laid down by this Court in S. Kasi Vs.
State, through Inspector of Police8.   
15. Also, in the impugned judgment, the Bombay High Court has noted other
7 PMLA
8 (2021) 12 SCC 1
4

## Page 271

significant  features  of  the  case,  in  great  detail,  and  recorded  findings  for
denying the benefit of the order dated 10th January, 2022 to the Enforcement
Directorate. We  need  not  refer  the  same  here,  having  regard  to  the  order
proposed  to  be  passed  by  us,  but  record  that  such  findings  have  our  full
concurrence.  
16. We, thus, uphold the impugned judgment as well as the decision of the
Calcutta High Court referred to above and over-rule the law, if any, laid down in
the decision of the Delhi High Court notwithstanding that the special leave
petition against it has been dismissed (without a reasoned order). 
17. It is, however, clarified that the petitioners before the Delhi High Court will
not be entitled to reopen proceedings citing this order.
18. Vide the impugned judgment, the Bombay High Court has vacated the

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.            OF 2026
DIARY NO.59959 OF 2026
MAHESH KUMAR DHIDHARIA APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
UNION OF INDIA & ORS. RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Delay condoned.
2. The appellant has filed an Original Application (OA) before
the National Green Tribunal, Central Zonal Bench, Bhopal (NGT),
alleging blatant disregard of the conditions stipulated in the
Environmental Clearance (EC) and Consent to Operate (CTO) by
respondent  No.7,  to  whom  the  Mining  Lease  No.323/1997  for
extraction of masonry stone in Village Tanwara, District Nagaur had
been granted.
3. Respondent No.7 had originally obtained CTO from Rajasthan
State Pollution Control Board on 20.11.2023, followed by EC granted
by the SEIAA on 14.06.2024.  
4. The OA was subsequently filed by the appellant, alleging that
respondent No.7 was carrying out mining activities, including deep-
hole blasting, within a close distance of 300 meters from the
residential areas, which was endangering the nearby public and
private property, besides causing environmental damage. Violations
of the conditions contained in the CTO and the EC were also
alleged.
1

## Page 278

5. The  NGT  constituted  a  Joint  Committee,  comprising
representatives  of  the  Central  Pollution  Control  Board  and
Rajasthan State Pollution Control Board, to inspect the mining site
and examine the allegations. The Joint Committee conducted a site
inspection on 23.07.2025 and undertook an elaborate and extensive
survey of the entire area. In its comprehensive report, the Joint
Committee found that respondent No.7 possessed a valid EC and CTO,
and there was no instance of non-compliance with the conditions
contained in those statutory permissions. No illegal mining was
found to have taken place. The Joint Committee also found that
instead of deep-hole blasting, only shallow-hole blasting was
practised.
6. Nevertheless,  the  Joint  Committee,  keeping  in  view  the
environmental issues and the vicinity of the village and its
residents, made certain recommendations contained in Paragraph 14.0
of its report, which the NGT has also reproduced in Paragraph 6 of
the impugned judgment. The recommendations are to the following
effect:
“14.0 Recommendations
i. Directorate General of Mines Safety (DGMS) may be
directed to conduct a detailed vibration/seismic study
to assess cumulative impact during operation of all 07
mines at a time.
ii. All leaseholders to install adequate hooter/siren
systems with standardized, high-decibel, multi-point
alarm systems, compliant with DGMS safety norms.
All the leaseholders shall optimize the frequency and
interval of blasting events to allow adequate dust
settling and minimize cumulative vibration and noise
impacts.
2

## Page 279

iv. All the leaseholders shall provide wind-braking
wall  of  MS  sheets  around  the  mine  lease  boundary
excluding entry & exit point to prevent unauthorized
entry and mitigate probable dust emission and ensure
safety.
Department  of  Mines  and  Geology  and  RSPCB  may  be
directed to take action on M/s Bajrang Lal S/o Kesar
ram (ML no. 48/2005) against exceeding its production
in FY 2023-24.
v. RSPCB need to conduct periodic Ambient air & noise
monitoring in and around the mining cluster and other
prominent locations.”
7. The NGT, while disposing of the OA, however, has restricted
its  directions  only  to  the  extent  of  directing  the  Project
Proponent, with the object of dust suppression, to increase the
plantation on the available land around the mining area and to
ensure the survival of the saplings for up to three years. The
State Pollution Control Board has been directed to periodically
monitor the plantation and its survival and take necessary action
in the event of non-compliance.
8. The aggrieved appellant has filed this statutory appeal.
9. We are conscious of the fact that neither any notice has been
issued  to  respondent  No.7-Project  Proponent,  nor  have  the
authorities been called upon to respond to the appeal at this
stage.However, it seems to us that it would be in the interest of
the village community and the Project Proponent, particularly for
the betterment of the environmental conditions in and around the
area, that all the recommendations made by the Joint Committee are
given effect by the authorities.
3

## Page 280

10. Consequently, we dispose of this appeal with a direction to
(i) the State of Rajasthan; (ii) the Rajasthan State Pollution
Control Board; (iii) the District Collector, Didwana-Kuchaman,
Rajasthan; and (iv) the Project Proponent, respondent No.7, to
ensure  that  the  remaining  recommendations  made  by  the  Joint
Committee in Paragraph 14.0 of their final report are also given
effect to. For this, the State Pollution Control Board will draw up
a necessary plan for implementation of the recommendations in a
time-bound manner and put up such plan before the NGT. The NGT may
ensure necessary compliance with the instant order.
11. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand closed.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA

CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.           OF 2026  
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) NO.14124/2026)
AMIR AHMAD KHAN      APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
STATE OF U.P.     RESPONDENT(S)
ORDER
1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard learned counsel for the appellant and
learned counsel for the respondent-State of Uttar Pradesh.
3. Appellant is aggrieved by the 2nd condition imposed by
the Chief Judicial Magistrate, Mirzapur, Uttar Pradesh
vide  order  dated  28.07.2025  in  Case  No.07/2024,  as
affirmed vide the impugned order dated 03.07.2026 by the
High Court of Judicature at Allahabad (briefly ‘the High
Court’ hereinafter).
4. Appellant is the victim of a cyber fraud, pursuant to
which he lodged FIR leading to registration of Case Crime
No.07/2024 under Sections 419 and 420 of the Indian Penal
Code, 1860 (for short, ‘IPC’) read with Section 66D of the
Information Technology Act, 2000.
5. Following investigation, a report was submitted by
the  In-charge  Inspector,  Cyber  Crime  Police  Station,
Mirzapur  before  the  Chief  Judicial  Magistrate  on
24.02.2025  regarding  the  amount  frozen  in  banks  in
1

## Page 283

connection with the aforesaid case. It was mentioned that
during investigation, it came to light that funds were
transferred through the account numbers mentioned in the
report, some of which were frozen by the concerned Banks.
The In-charge Inspector stated that all the aforesaid
accounts had been frozen under Section 102 of the Code of
Criminal Procedure, 1973 (for short, ‘CrPC’). However,
having regard to the investigation carried out, it would
be just and proper to release the said money in favour of
the complainant (appellant herein).
6. Chief  Judicial  Magistrate,  Mirzapur  passed  order
dated  28.07.2025,  after  recording  that  a  total  of
Rs.7,12,060/- has been frozen in the 23 bank accounts
mentioned in the report directed release of the aforesaid
amount of Rs.7,12,060/- to the account of the appellant,
subject to the conditions that appellant should submit a
personal bond of Rs.7,12,060/- and one security of the
same amount.
7. When this was assailed by the appellant before the
High Court, by the impugned order dated 03.07.2026, the
High Court took the view that there was no need for any
modification  in  the  conditions  imposed  by  the  Chief
Judicial  Magistrate  and  accordingly,  dismissed  the
application of the appellant.
8. After hearing learned counsel for the parties, we are
of the view that non-release of the aforesaid amount in
favour of the appellant, who is himself a victim of cyber
2

## Page 284

fraud, would result in causing further harassment to the
appellant. We take note of the fact that appellant is aged
about 80 years and at this stage, requiring him to furnish
security of Rs.7,12,060/-, would not be just and proper.
Such a condition would be harsh and oppressive.
9. We, accordingly, set aside the 2nd condition imposed
by the Chief Judicial Magistrate, Mirzapur in the order
dated 28.07.2025, and the impugned order dated 03.07.2026
passed by the High Court. We direct that the amount of
Rs.7,12,060/- shall be released in favour of the appellant
on furnishing of a Personal Bond of Rs.7,12,060/- by the
appellant, within a period of two weeks from today.
10. Consequently, the Criminal Appeal is allowed.
11. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

CRIMINAL APPEAL NOS.5341-5342 OF 2026
(@SLP(CRL.) NOS. 20002-20003 OF 2026)
GURJODH SINGH ..... APPELLANT(S)
              VERSUS
STATE OF PUNJAB  ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Heard.
2. Leave granted.
3. Appellant who has been visited with FIR No.39 dated 24.02.2023
registered at Police Station Ajnala, District Amritsar, for the offences
punishable under Sections 307, 353, 186, 332, 333, 506(ii),120-B, 427,
148 and 149 of the IPC and Sections 25/27 of the Arms Act, 1959 and
Section 201 IPC, which was subsequently added, is seeking for grant
of regular bail. 
4. The prosecution case arises out of an incident that occurred on
23.02.2023 by a mob of approximately 200-250 persons allegedly led
by  Amritpal Singh and armed with deadly weapons reached Ajnala
Police Station for securing the release of their associate. The said mob
is said to have attacked the police personnel including senior officers
causing injuries and is said to have vandalised the property. Though
1                                                          SLP(CRL.) NOS. 20002-20003 OF 2026

## Page 295

appellant was not named in the FIR, prosecution subsequently alleged
that appellant was also armed with a satta/dang (stick) and he had
broken the barricade along with others and participated in the incident
and thereafter threw the stick away. However, it is the contention of
the  learned  counsel  appearing  for  appellant  that  his  presence  at
Ajanala, itself is in serious dispute, inasmuch as his mobile, which has
been seized by the jurisdictional police, would clearly place him at
Chogawan,  a  place  which  is  15  kms  away  from  the  place  of  the
incident.
5. Appellant  has  been  in  custody  since  18.03.2023.  Earlier
applications of the appellant having been dismissed by the High Court
and also by this Court granting liberty to the appellant to renew his
prayer for bail if trial is not concluded within six months, the present
appeals have been filed.
6. Though the learned counsel appearing for the respondent-State
would vehemently and strongly oppose the grant of bail contending
interalia that appellant had not only indulged in the acts as alleged in
the FIR but was also part of the mob which pulled down the police
station and as such he is not entitled for grant of bail, we are not
inclined to entertain the said contention inasmuch as the incident has
taken place way back on 23.02.2023 and this Court while rejecting or
dismissing SLP (Crl) No.14561/2024 on 19.12.2024 had granted liberty
to the appellant to renew his prayer if trial is not concluded within six
months. Undisputedly trial is not concluded. The prosecution has filed
an  application  before  the  jurisdictional  High  Court  seeking  for
2                                                          SLP(CRL.) NOS. 20002-20003 OF 2026

## Page 296

extension of time and in the order passed on 13.05.2026 the High
Court has acceded to said request and has granted four months time
to conclude the trial. In other words trial has not concluded.
7. In  these  circumstances,  we  are  of  the  considered  view  that
continued incarceration of the appellant would not be warranted and
he  is  ordered  to  be  released  on  regular  bail  on  such  terms  and
conditions as the jurisdictional Court may deem fit to impose including
the condition of directing the appellant to mark his attendance before
the jurisdictional Court once in 15 days till the conclusion of the trial.
Accordingly, the appeals stand allowed.
8. It is also made clear that appellant shall cooperate with the trial
and shall not seek any adjournment on any ground whatsoever and if
such request were to be made, the trial court would be at liberty to
consider the prayer of the prosecution for cancellation of the bail, in
the event of such application being filed.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.       OF 2026
(arising out of SLP(C) No. 16669/2026)
RAJ GOYAL ..... APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
PRADEEP JADHAV ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted. 
2. The appellant, Raj Goyal, is aggrieved by the order dated
23.03.2026 passed by the High Court of Madhya Pradesh at
Gwalior in Misc. Petition No. 3656/2025. By the said order,
the High Court, having observed that the decree in question
required the defendant, the appellant before us, to execute
the  sale  deed  within  six  months  after  receiving  the
consideration, proceeded to hold that in terms of Section 28
of the Specific Relief Act, 19631, the executing Court could
not introduce conditions which did not form part of the
decree. Having stated so, the High Court strangely observed
that no obligation was cast upon the plaintiff/decree-holder,
the respondent herein, to pay the consideration amount within
a specified time.  Based on this understanding of the decree,
the High Court directed the executing Court to proceed with
1  “the 1963 Act” for short
1

## Page 315

the execution petition filed for execution of the sale deed in
accordance with the decree in question. 
3. By order dated 15.05.2026, this Court granted stay of the
impugned order dated 23.03.2026. 
4. The decree in question is dated 21.11.2022 and relates to an
agreement to sell dated 21.09.2020. Pursuant to the said
agreement to sell, the respondent had paid 1,01,000/- (Rupees₹
one  lakh  one  thousand  only)  out  of  the  total  sale
consideration of 34,21,000/- (Rupees thirty four lakhs twenty₹
one thousand only). The specific performance suit filed by the
respondent was decreed on 21.11.2022, directing that the sale
deed shall be executed by the appellant within six months upon
the respondent paying the remaining amount of consideration
viz. 33,20,000/- (Rupees thirty three lakhs twenty thousand₹
only) along with the registration expenses. The decree also
made it clear that if the sale deed was still not executed by
the appellant within six months, the respondent would be
entitled to get the sale deed executed through Court.
5. It is an admitted fact that the respondent did not make any
offer within the stipulated six months’ period to pay the
balance sale consideration and the registration expenses. It
was  only  in  the  seventh  month  that  the  respondent,
straightaway filed an execution petition.
6. It is now argued before us on behalf of the respondent that as
the appellant had filed an appeal, no steps were taken by him.
However, it is an admitted fact that the filing of the appeal
2

## Page 316

by the appellant came to the notice of the respondent only
after the filing of the execution petition, that is, after the
expiry of the stipulated six months’ period. 
7. When the decree in question specifically noted that the
appellant would be under an obligation to execute the sale
deed upon receiving the balance sale consideration and the
registration  expenses  within  the  stipulated  six  months’
period, the duty was first cast upon the respondent to pay the
said amount within that time. It was only upon such payment
being made that the appellant was under an obligation to
execute the sale deed. No steps were ever taken by the
respondent to even offer such payment and the High court
erroneously held to the contrary that there was no obligation
cast upon him. It was, in fact, the High Court which rewrote
the terms of the decree, a course which was not open to it. 
8. The  appeal  is,  accordingly,  allowed,  setting  aside  the
impugned order passed by the High Court. In the light of what
we have held above, the decree would be inexecutable, in terms
of Section 28 of the 1963 Act. 
     Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of. 
     Parties shall bear their own costs.
