1. Leave granted.
2. This appeal is directed against a judgment and order dated 17th
September, 2025 passed by the High Court of Calcutta partially allowing
a criminal revisional application1 of the respondents. 
3. Appellant  had  lodged  a  complaint2 before  the  Additional  Chief
Judicial Magistrate3, Barrackpore, North 24 Parganas, West Bengal. By
the impugned order, the High Court has directed the trial magistrate as
under: -
“30. Hence, I remit the matter to the Magistrate for passing fresh order
uninfluenced by any observation made herein. The order impugned dated
04.03.2017  and  all  subsequent  orders  are  hereby  set  aside.  Learned
Magistrate  is  directed  to  form  a  Medical  Board  of  experts  in  the
concerned faculties comprising of at least three medical officers of which
one must be qualified in Orthopaedic Science and who are employed in
government service and who can normally be expected to give impartial
and unbiased opinion and thereafter he will send all medical documents
including  complaint  and  the  documents  annexed  with  the  petition  of
complaint and other medical documents, if any relied by the complainant,
so  that  Board  can  form  a  definite  opinion  in  the  guideline  given  in
paragraph  52  of  the  judgment  passed  in  Jacob  Mathew  (supra).  The
opposite party herein shall be at liberty to produce all the medical papers
he want to rely before the court below within a period of eight weeks from
the date of the order and on receipt of such documents, the magistrate
concerned will seek such opinion from the concerned Board and after
1  CRR No.2327 of 2018
2  No.2 of 2017
3  trial magistrate
1

## Page 343

obtaining opinion from the Medical Board and after considering complaint
along with annexure, initial deposition and opinion of Medical Board he
will proceed for the next step in accordance with law.”
4. We have heard the appellant appearing in-person as well as Mr.
Rana  Mukherjee,  learned  senior  counsel  for  the  respondents  duly
assisted by Mr. Partha Sil, learned counsel.
5. In course of a previous hearing, we had called for the records of
CRR No.2327 of 2018 from the High Court to satisfy ourselves that the
respondents had approached the High Court with full particulars and
clean hands.
6. We  find  that  a  couple  of  reports  were  not  disclosed  by  the
respondents in the criminal revision application.
7. In such view of the matter, the High Court was in error and ought
not to have even partially allowed the criminal revisional application.
8. Accordingly, the impugned judgment and order stands set aside.
9. The trial magistrate may now proceed with the complaint lodged by
the  appellant from the stage the  proceedings  had reached, prior  to
interference by the High Court in the revisional application.
10. Since the complaint is dated 03rd January, 2017, interest of justice
would require disposal thereof in accordance with law, as expeditiously
as possible.
11. The trial magistrate is encouraged to expedite its decision after
conclusion of trial at an early date.

STATE OF ODISHA                                    Respondent(s)
O R D E R 
1. Leave granted.
2. Heard learned counsel for the parties.
3. This appeal impugns the order dated 20.11.2025 passed by
the High Court of Odisha whereby the application of the
appellant for suspension of sentence pending consideration of
his appeal against the order of the trial court has been
rejected. 
4. The submission on behalf of the appellant is that the
appellant was prosecuted inter alia for an offence punishable
under the provisions of the Protection of Children from Sexual
Offences (‘POCSO) Act, 2012. However, conviction was not under
the POCSO Act as the victim was not found to be a minor.
Rather, the appellant was convicted under Section 376(1) of
the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short ‘IPC’) and sentenced to
10 year R.I. It is submitted that the victim and the accused
1

## Page 355

are of the same village; the First Information Report of the
case was lodged with delay; there was no medical corroboration
to the allegations; and from the evidence on record, it
appears  there  was  an  effort  for  settlement.  In  such
circumstances, while deciding the appeal the High Court would
have to consider not only whether the victim was sexually
assaulted but also whether there was some kind of consensual
relationship between the accused and the victim. It has also
been submitted that the appellant has suffered over three
years of incarceration whereas the sentence awarded to him is
of ten years and there is no likelihood of the appeal being
decided in near future.      
5. The learned counsel for the respondent-State has opposed
the prayer for suspension of sentence by submitting that the
trial court has convicted the appellant after considering and
analyzing the evidence; therefore, any observations on merits
might prejudice the High Court while deciding the pending
criminal appeal of the appellant.
6. Having regard to the submissions noticed above, without
expressing any opinion on the merits thereof, while taking
into  consideration  that  the  appellant  has  suffered
incarceration for a period exceeding three years, we are of
the view that the appellant has made out a case for suspension
of sentence pending consideration of his appeal by the High
2

## Page 356

Court. 
7. Consequently, the appeal is allowed. The order rejecting
the prayer for suspension of sentence is set aside. The
sentence awarded by the Trial Court shall remain suspended
pending consideration of appellant’s appeal by the High Court.
8. The appellant shall be released on bail pending disposal
of his appeal by the High Court on such terms and conditions
as the trial court may deem fit to impose in the facts and
circumstances of the case. 
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

1. Though there is a delay of 255 days in filing this appeal,
we have nevertheless heard learned senior counsel for the
appellant. We have also perused the application seeking
condonation  of  delay.  The  reasons  for  the  delay  are
explained in the application as under:-
“3. That the impugned judgment and order was passed
on 28.11.2025. Since, the Sahara Group is facing
multiple  actions/investigations  and  overall,
distressed situation, some time was consumed in
arranging the relevant documents and taking steps
for filing the Appeal. It is pertinent to mention
that various employees of Sahara Group have left
their  employment  and  therefore,  some  time  was
consumed in getting the appeal prepared and filed.
Thus,  inadvertently  delay  of  255  days  has
occasioned  in  filing  the  Appeal  which  is  not
deliberate or intentional. As such, through the
instant application, the benevolent indulgence of
this Hon’ble Court is sought for condoning the
delay of 255 days in filing the accompanying Appeal
under Section 18 of the TRAI Act.”
2. On consideration of the same, we find that the explanation
offered for seeking condonation of delay in filing this
appeal is neither satisfactory nor sufficient in law so as
to  condone  the  delay  in  filing  this  appeal.  In  the
circumstances,  we  dismiss  the  application  seeking
condonation of delay.

ground of delay.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL  NO.               OF 2026
(@ SLP(CRL.) No. 20572/2026)
 UPENDRA SAHU                      APPELLANT(S)
                         VERSUS
STATE OF CHHATTISGARH           RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1.  Leave granted. 
2.  The appellant has been arraigned as an accused
and seeks regular bail in connection with FIR
No.31/2026,  registered  at  Police  Station  –
Rajim,  District  Gariabandh  for  the  offences
punishable under Sections 296, 115(2), 351(3),
332(b), 332(c), 109(1), 190, 191(2), 191(3) and
326(g) of the Bhartiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
3.  We  have  heard  the  learned  Senior  Counsel
appearing for the appellant and the learned
counsel appearing for the respondent – State.
4.  Learned  Senior  Counsel  appearing  for  the
appellant submitted that apart from the period
of incarceration, there is no specific overt act
against the appellant and he is only 21 years
1

## Page 379

old. In any case, it is submitted that it is a
case where charges for lesser offence alone is
made out, even assuming that the prosecution
proved the case.
5.  Learned  counsel  appearing  for  the  State
submitted that considering the fact that the
appellant has been arraigned as an accused in
the  FIR  itself,  there  is  no  need  for  any
interference. 
6.  Admittedly, the charge-sheet has been filed and
the charges have been framed. Suffice it is to
state  that  continued  incarceration  of  the
appellant is no longer required. The appellant
has no antecedents and he is only 21 years old. 
7.  Considering the above, we are inclined to set
aside the impugned order passed by the High
Court, and grant bail to the appellant.
8.  Accordingly,  the  impugned  order  stands  set
aside, and the appellant is granted regular
bail, subject to the terms and conditions that
may be imposed by the concerned Trial Court. 
9.  The appeal is allowed, accordingly.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The petitioners before this Court have filed the
present petitions, being aggrieved by the impugned order
dated  06.05.2026 passed by the High Court of Punjab &
Haryana at Chandigarh in CRM-M Nos. 4760 and 14732 of 2026,
rejecting the prayer for anticipatory bail in connection
with FIR No. 02 of 2026, registered at Police Station GRP
Sirhind,  District  Government  Railway  Police  (Fatehgarh
Sahib), for the offences punishable under Sections 108 and
3(5) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
2. This Court, vide order dated 03.07.2026, granted
interim  protection  to  the  petitioners  in  the  matter.
Pursuant thereto, the petitioner has participated in the
investigation and has appeared before the Investigating
Officer on as many as ten occasions.
3. Although the prayer for grant of anticipatory bail
has been opposed by learned counsel for respondent No. 2,
taking into consideration the fact that the petitioner has
2

## Page 391

joined  the  investigation  and  appeared  before  the
Investigating Officer as many as ten times, this Court, in
the peculiar facts and circumstances of the case, is of the
opinion that the interim order dated 03.07.2026 deserves to
be made absolute.
4. Accordingly, interim order dated 03.07.2026 is made
absolute subject to the condition that petitioners shall
continue to co-operate with the investigation and shall
report  as  and  when  called  upon  to  do  so  by  the
Investigating Authority.
5. The Special Leave Petitions are accordingly disposed
of in the above terms.
6. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand
disposed of.

on 12.10.2026 to file a reply. However, no reply has been

## Page 393

filed till date.
2. Leave granted.
3. The  appellant  before  this  Court  has  filed  the
present appeal, being aggrieved by the impugned judgment
dated  10.02.2023 passed by the High Court of Orissa at
Cuttack in JCRLA No. 55 of 2021, whereby the conviction and
sentence of life imprisonment imposed upon the appellant
under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, by the
Additional Sessions Judge, Talcher in C.T. (S) No. 14 of
2016 arising out of G.R. Case No. 144 of 2015, were
affirmed.
4. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that the
appellant is suffering from schizophrenia and has already
undergone 11 years of actual incarceration.
5. Learned counsel appearing for the respondent-State
has opposed the prayer for suspension of sentence.
6. After  careful  consideration  of  the  documents  on
record and having heard learned counsel for the parties,
this Court is of the opinion that the prayer for suspension
of sentence deserves to be allowed. Accordingly, the prayer
is allowed.
7. Accordingly,  the  execution  of  the  substantive
sentence of imprisonment awarded to the appellant shall
remain suspended during the pendency of the appeal, and he
2

is directed to be released on bail subject to such terms
and conditions as may be imposed by the Trial Court.
8. Let the original records of the Trial Court be
requisitioned.
9. List the appeal for hearing in due course.

Date : 16-11-2026 This matter was called on for hearing today.
CORAM :  HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE JOYMALYA BAGCHI
         HON'BLE MRS. JUSTICE V. MOHANA
For Petitioner(s) :Mr. Vipin Sanghi, Sr. Adv.
                   Mr. Prateek A. Rajurkar, Adv.
                   Mr. Satyajit A. Desai, Adv.
                   Mr. Shashank Upadhyay, Adv.
                   Mr. Pratik Kumar Singh, Adv.
                   Mr. Sachin Singh, Adv.
                   Ms. Anagha S. Desai- 1588, AOR
                   
For Respondent(s) : 
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Delay condoned.
2. We have considered the submissions of Mr. Vipin Sanghi,
learned Senior Counsel, to the effect that Rule XII of the
Maharashtra Zilla Parishads and Panchayat Samitis Rules, 2025 (in
1

## Page 441

short, ‘2025 Rules’), by shifting the cut-off date for rotation of
constituencies for the purposes of reservation, renders the very
concept of rotation of reserved seats illusory. 
3. Though the argument is attractive at first blush, it fails to
take into consideration the fact that no voter or candidate can
claim a vested right to have a particular constituency reserved.
What the Constitution and the State Act prescribe is proportionate
reservation  of  seats  vis-à-vis  the  proportion  of  the  SC/ST
population to the total population in the local body concerned. It
is nobody's case that the reservation of seats for SCs/STs is not
in proportion to their population.
4. It is also correct that the law prescribes rotation of the
reserved seats in the descending order of the SC/ST population.
However, the manner and time frame within which such rotation is to
be carried out is within the discretion of the Government. In
exercise of such discretion, Rule XII of the 2025 Rules prescribes
the next election following the 2025 Rules shall be treated as the
first election for the purpose of rotation of reserved seats. 
5. We find no reason to hold that the said Rule runs counter
either to the concept of reservation or the principle of rotation
of seats.
6. Needless to mention that the dismissal of the petition shall
not stand in the way of the petitioner making a representation
seeking reconsideration of the scheme for rotation of reserved
seats in accordance with law.
2

## Page 442

7. The Special Leave Petition is, accordingly, dismissed.
8. Pending applications, if any, also stand disposed of.

1

## Page 450

                        O R D E R
IA NO. 334375/2025
The present SLP arises out of a common judgment
and order passed by the Delhi High Court in a bunch
of  11  writ  petitions.  This  is  an  IA  seeking
clarification/modification of the interim order dated
17th  February 2025 which is reproduced here under :
“Issue  notice,  returnable  in  the  week
commencing 28.04.2025. 
Notice  is  accepted  by  Mr.  Anshuman
Srivastava, learned counsel, who is present on
advance notice/caveat for respondent no. 1.
Hence, notice need not be served on the said
respondent. Respondent no. 2 is a proforma
respondent and need not be served.
Counter  affidavit/reply  shall  be  filed
within  four  weeks  from  today.  Rejoinder
affidavit, if any, may be filed within three
weeks  after  service  of  the  counter
affidavit/reply. 
We are informed that the petitioner
will  be  filing  special  leave  petition(s)
against the impugned judgment in the context of
the other writ petitions which have also been
allowed.
Without prejudice to the rights and
contentions of the petitioner, in cases where
there were no Audit Quality Review Reports
(AQRR) prepared and no final orders have been
passed, the proceedings may continue but no
final orders will be passed. We clarify that
2

## Page 451

where  final  orders  have  been  passed,  such
orders will not be given effect to.”
Mr. N Venkataraman, learned Additional Solicitor
General  appearing  for  the  petitioner-applicant
submits that it may be clarified that the interim
order dated 17th February 2025 is confined only to the
parties to the 11 writ petitions decided by the
common judgment and order of the Delhi High Court
impugned in the present SLP.
In our considered opinion, there is no need
for any clarification.  It goes without saying that
any interim order passed in the petition pending
before this Court relates only to and is confined to
the parties to the 11 petitions decided by the High
Court vide impugned judgment and order.
The application stands disposed of.
(SONIA BHASIN)
ASSISTANT REGISTRAR-CUM-PS
(RANJANA SHAILEY)
ASSISTANT REGISTRAR

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The submission on behalf of the petitioners is that
the gravamen of the allegation in the impugned First
Information Report is regarding non-performance of the
Share Subscription Agreement by the accused company.  It
is submitted that the right under the Share Subscription
Agreement had to be exercised within three years.  The
agreement  did  not  carry  any  clause  whereunder  the
complainant party had a right to seek for extension of
time  to  exercise  its  right  of  purchase/subscription.
Admittedly, the complainant party, before expiry of the
period within which the subscription right had to be
exercised, had served a notice whereunder they had sought
extension  of  time  to  exercise  that  right.  In  such
circumstances, if the extension had been denied, it cannot
be a ground to infer that there had been a dishonest
intention from the very beginning. Consequently, it is
argued, the First Information Report does not disclose
commission of a cognizable offence and, therefore, is
liable to the quashed.  In addition, it has been submitted
2

## Page 484

that the agreement provided a procedure for amendment by
specifically disclosing that all amendments would have to
be in writing. In  such  circumstances,  allegations  that
there had been assurances given by the Director of the
accused  company  would  have  no  bearing  on  the
rights/liabilities of the parties.
2. Issue notice, returnable in six weeks.
3. Notice on behalf of respondent no.2 has been accepted
by Ms. Shivika Mehra, Advocate. 
4. In the meantime, no further action shall be taken
pursuant to the impugned First Information Report.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. By the impugned order, the High Court has remanded
the matter back to the Trial Court on the ground that the
1

## Page 489

accused was not given opportunity to cross-examine the
prosecution witnesses.
2. The submission on behalf of the petitioner is that
the  trial  was  under  Section  138  of  the  Negotiable
Instruments  Act,  1881  and,  therefore,  the  witnesses’
affidavits were admissible in evidence under Section 145 of
the said Act. Though, the Trial Court could have allowed
cross-examination of those witnesses, if it deemed fit, or
when there was an application from the side of the accused
for their cross-examination.
3. It has been submitted on behalf of the petitioner
that there is nothing on record to indicate that the
accused had requested the Court for cross-examining the
complainant witnesses.  In such circumstances, the High
Court fell in error in remanding the matter back to the
Trial Court on the ground that accused was not given
opportunity to cross-examine the prosecution witnesses.
4. A  counter  affidavit  has  been  filed  from  the
respondent’s side.  In the counter affidavit, there is no
specific averment that an application for cross-examining
the prosecution witnesses was submitted before the Court
and the same was either rejected or no orders was passed
thereon.
5. The learned counsel for the respondent(s), however,
prays for and is allowed three weeks’ time to file a better
affidavit disclosing specifically whether any application
was  submitted  by  the  accused  to  cross-examine  the
2

## Page 490

prosecution  witnesses.  If  any  such  application  was
submitted, whether the same was pressed or not and if
pressed, whether it was rejected by the Trial Court.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Delay condoned.
2. Exemption Applications are allowed.
3. This matter has come up today to consider the plea of the
petitioner (convict) for suspension of sentence of rigorous
imprisonment and release on bail, pending the final disposal

## Page 492

2
of his criminal appeal before the High Court.
4. It is alleged that the deceased, wife of complainant, was
abducted by the  petitioner  on 18.05.2018 against which a
missing complaint was filed. On 07.07.2018, the complainant
was informed that his wife was found dead by hanging at the
rented  accommodation  of  the  petitioner.  During
investigation, it came to light that the deceased was
allegedly having an affair with the petitioner.
5.We take notice of the fact that the petitioner was put to
trial for the offence punishable under Sections 306, 366 and
34 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short, “the IPC”).
The Trial Court, relying on the circumstantial evidence,
held  the  petitioner  guilty  of  the  alleged  crime  and
sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for 10 years
with fine of Rs.25,000/- (Rupees Twenty Five Thousand only),
in default to undergo simple imprisonment for one year in
S.T. No.157/2019 arising out of G.R. Case No.1434 of 2018,
Hazaribagh, corresponding to Korrah P.S. Case No.20 of 2018
of the Court of District and Additional Sessions Judge-VI,
Hazaribagh.
6.Being dissatisfied with the rejection of bail application by
the High Court, the petitioner filed this Special Leave
Petition before us.
7.We take notice of the fact that the petitioner is in jail
for almost two years, including the undertrial period.
Admittedly, the deceased had been living with the accused in

## Page 493

3
a rented house and the owners of the house, PW5 and PW6
deposed that they were informed that the couple were husband
and wife. It was also deposed that A1 was not present in the
house when the unfortunate incident of hanging occurred.  
 
8.On a prima facie consideration, we are of the opinion that
the sentence imposed on the petitioner can be suspended
pending the final disposal of his criminal appeal before the
High Court and the petitioner be released on bail for the
time being.
9.In view of the aforesaid, we suspend the substantive order
of sentence of 10 years of rigorous imprisonment and fine
imposed on the petitioner and order that the he be released
on bail forthwith, if not required in any other case,
subject to terms and conditions that the trial court may
deem fit to impose, pending the final disposal of his appeal
before the High Court.
10. The SLP is disposed of accordingly.
11. Pending applications, if any, also stand disposed of.

     UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The petitioner, has been in custody since 13.12.2024 and has
been denied regular bail by the High Court in connection with
FIR No. 307/2024 registered with Police Station Khanpur,
Haridwar, for the offence punishable under Sections 103(1),
238, 3(5) and 311 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (for short
“BNS”), 2023 respectively.
2. The petitioner, along with co-accused, is alleged to have
conspired to rob the deceased, during the course of which the
deceased  died.  The  petitioner  is  further  accused  of
facilitating the disposal of the dead body by arranging a
vehicle and transporting and burying the body.
3. The case rests entirely on the circumstantial evidence and
there  is  no  eyewitness’s  testimony.  The  investigation
proceeded on the confession statements made by the accused,
and it is for the Trial Court to consider whether the
circumstantial evidence is founded on valid incriminating
circumstances, bringing home the guilt of the accused.  
4. A charge sheet has been filed in this case including Section
309(4)  BNS,  wherein  it  is  recorded  that  the  petitioner
transferred money via UPI from the deceased’s phone under the
pretext of a medical emergency. Charges have been framed
against the petitioner for the aforesaid offences and the
trial is in progress. The prosecution has proposed to examine
33 witnesses out of which only 7 have been examined so far.
5. On a  prima facie consideration of the materials on record,
prolonged trial and after hearing the learned counsel for the
parties, we are of the opinion that the petitioner can be
released on bail, subject to such terms and conditions that
the Additional District and Sessions Judge, Laksar, Haridwar
(the  jurisdictional  court)  may  deem  fit  to  impose.  The
petitioner shall cooperate with the trial.
6. With the above directions, the Special Leave Petition is
disposed of.

For Petitioner(s) :Petitioner-in-person
                    
For Respondent(s) :Mr. B. Karunakaran- 3845, AOR
                   Mr. Bharthi Subramanian, Adv.
                   Mr. Fazil, Adv.
                   Ms. Jeyashree, Adv.
                   Ms. Balambika, Adv.                  
                   
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. We have heard the party appearing in person for a reasonable time. It is
contended that several complaints though lodged, none of his complaints are
being investigated. He also contends that his fundamental rights are infringed
and as such he had approached the jurisdictional High Court for redressal of his
grievance.
1

## Page 657

2. It is in this background, we have perused the impugned judgment and
order which reveals that High Court has made an endeavour to ascertain from
the learned Government Advocate as to the status of the petitioner’s complaint
and has recorded that complaint lodged by petitioner has been enquired into
and closed. Yet the High Court has given liberty to the petitioner to lodge  fresh
complaint on a fresh cause of action before the jurisdictional Police and has also
directed the jurisdictional police to enquire into such complaints with a time
frame and accordingly the petition has been disposed of by the High Court.
3. That apart, we notice that the petitioner has been approaching this Court
on a number of occasions and this Court in Miscellaneous Application Diary No.
13409/2024 by order dated 30.08.2024 has observed as:-
“5. The petitioner has informed this Court that now he
is law graduate. He candidly acknowledges that earlier he
had 42 mobile numbers and about 15 bank accounts. That
being so, it would be expedient and in the interest of
justice that the petitioner appears before the Trial Court
and extends full cooperation in pending proceedings.”
4. The above orders passed by the High Court as well as by this Court would
sufficiently protect the right of the petitioner and as such question of granting
any relief in these petitions would not arise. Hence, the Special Leave Petitions
stand dismissed.
5. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of. 
    (DEEPANSHU)                          (AVGV RAMU)
SENIOR PERSONAL ASSISTANT             COURT MASTER (NSH)

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The petitioner who is the successful claimant before the arbitral
tribunal is before this Court.
1

## Page 683

2. Being aggrieved by the order of the High Court whereunder the
appeal filed under Section 37 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act,
1996 is being adjudicated, by directing partial deposit of award amount
contending  inter alia that entire award amount with interest has not
been ordered to be deposited and as such interest of petitioner is not
being secured.
3. The record speaks for itself namely the Appellate Court has directed
the  unsuccessful  respondent/defendant  to  deposit  a  sum  of  Rs.12.5
crores with interest as awarded by the arbitral tribunal and accordingly,
the same is said to have been deposited and the order of interim stay of
the award has been confirmed.
4. However, the successful claimant is being aggrieved as the entire
award amount having not been ordered to be paid or deposited and to
the extent of the non-securing of the entire award amount, the present
petition has been filed.
5. Any scrutiny or examination of rival contentions on merits is likely
to prejudice the rights of either of the parties in the pending appeal. As
such we desist from examining the claim on merits. However, it would
suffice to request to jurisdictional High Court to expedite the hearing of
the  appeal preferably  within  a  period  of  two  months  subject  to  the
learned counsel appearing for both the parties cooperating. 
6. Accordingly, the present petition stands disposed of.
7. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of.

                                VERSUS
UNION OF INDIA & ORS.                              Respondent(s)
Date : 16-11-2026 This petition was called on for hearing today.
CORAM :  HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE JOYMALYA BAGCHI
         HON'BLE MRS. JUSTICE V. MOHANA
For Petitioner(s) :  Petitioner-in-person
                    
For Respondent(s) : 
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The petitioner has approached this Court relying upon the
Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG) Report, which
highlights deficiencies in sanitation and maintenance of various
passenger amenities at railway stations across the country. The
petitioner seeks directions to the authorities with regard to the
provision of safe and hygienic drinking water, cleanliness and
sanitation,  functional  toilets,  proper  waste  management,
accessibility, emergency medical facilities, and other prescribed
minimum essential amenities at railway stations, within a time-
bound manner.
2. We note that a similar representation had been submitted to
the authorities concerned in September 2026.
3. While we are of the considered view that the nature of
grievances flagged by the petitioner are of substantial public
1

## Page 805

interest, we also take note of the fact that the authorities may
require reasonable time to examine the recommendations made in the
CAG report and the other issues raised by the petitioner.
4. Accordingly, we direct the petitioner to pursue the aforesaid
representation before the authorities concerned, who shall look
into the same and take appropriate remedial measures, as may be
necessary, to ensure the health and safety of passengers availing
railway services.
5. With liberty aforesaid, the Writ Petition is disposed of.
6. Pending applications, if any, also stand disposed of.
(ARJUN BISHT)                              (PREETHI DILEEP KUMAR)

IA No. 343812/2026 - EXEMPTION FROM FILING C/C OF THE IMPUGNED 
JUDGMENT
 
Date : 17-11-2026 This matter was called on for hearing today.
CORAM :  HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE MANOJ MISRA
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE VIJAY BISHNOI
For Petitioner(s) :Mr. K M Natraj, A.S.G.
                   Mr. Merusagar Samantaray- 1694, AOR
                   Mr. Anurag Yadav, Adv.
                   Ms. Tharani Sre, Adv.
                                      
For Respondent(s) :Mr. Krishnamohan K.- 2561, AOR
                   Ms. Prerna Jain Kala, Adv.
                   Ms. Pragati Tiwari, Adv.
                         
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Delay in refiling this special leave petition is
condoned.
2. The submission on behalf of the petitioner is
that admittedly the term of the contract had expired
therefore  the  issue  was  whether  the  original
applicant was entitled for renewal of the contract.
Under the terms of the bye-laws, the renewal was
dependent on Review Committee’s assessment report.
1

## Page 837

In paragraph 9.5 of the judgment of the Central
Administrative Tribunal (for short ‘the Tribunal’),
the Tribunal notices that the Review Committee’s
assessment  report  had  declared  the  original
applicant “below average” and “unfit” yet the Review
Committee’s assessment was overlooked on the ground
that the order dispensing with the service did not
recite such assessment as the basis for dispensation
of service; it stated that the contract period had
expired by efflux by time. It is submitted that such
approach is erroneous in law and, therefore, the
High Court ought to have stayed the effect and
operation of the order passed by the Tribunal.
3. Issue notice, returnable in six weeks.
4. Notice on behalf of the respondent(s) has been
accepted by Mr. Krishnamohan K., AOR.
5. In the meantime, the effect and operation of the
order passed by the Tribunal shall remain stayed.
6. It  is,  however,  made  clear  that  further
proceedings on the writ petition pending before the
High Court has not been stayed. The High Court may
proceed with the writ petition and take its own
decision without being prejudiced by any observation
made in this order.
  
(CHETAN ARORA)                                  (SAPNA BANSAL)
ASTT. REGISTRAR-cum-PS                        COURT MASTER (NSH)

CORAM : 
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE MANOJ MISRA

For Petitioner(s)  Mr. Manish Kumar, Adv.

                   Ms. Pooja Soni, Adv.
                   Mr. Sachin Saini- 3697, AOR
                   
                   Mr. Niteen Kumar Sinha- 3262, AOR
                   
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The submission on behalf of the petitioner is that
pay and recover principle can only be applied where there
is a subsisting insurance policy.  Here, the Motor Accident
Claims Tribunal while deciding issue (va) has recorded a
1

## Page 1029

specific finding that the vehicle was not insured and this
finding has been confirmed by the High Court in paragraph
20 of its judgment.  In such circumstances, reliance upon a
three Judge Bench decision of this Court in  Oriental
Insurance Co.Ltd. vs. Inderjit Kaur & Ors., (1998) 1 SCC
371 was not warranted as that judgment dealt with a fact
situation  wherein  on  account  of  non-payment  of  the
insurance premium, the insurance policy was not cancelled.
Whereas in the present case the insurance policy was
cancelled prior to the date of the accident.
2. Delay condoned.
3. Issue notice, returnable in six weeks.
4. Mr. Sachin Saini, Advocate accepts notice on behalf
of Respondent No.3.
5. In the meantime, the award against the petitioner
shall remain stayed.  However, the claimants – respondents
are at liberty to recover the awarded amount from the
owner/driver of the offending vehicle.

intention of deceiving the public and extorting money from them
under the pretext of implicating them in false criminal cases. The
petitioner is not named in the above mentioned FIR. The High Court
denied him anticipatory bail on the ground that the petitioner had
allegedly  threatened  persons/witnesses  in  connection  with  the
involvement of the co-accused in the alleged illegal activities.  
3. Notice was issued by us on 15.10.2026, with a direction that
no coercive steps shall be taken against the petitioner, subject to
his cooperation with the investigation. This Court by Order dated
30.10.2026 extended the interim protection.
4. The Learned Counsel for the State has also submitted that the
petitioner is cooperating with the investigation.
5. Upon prima facie consideration of the material on record, the
fact that multiple FIRs of a similar nature have been registered
against unknown persons without any specific allegations, and the
fact that the High Court granted anticipatory bail to a similarly
situated co-accused, we are of the opinion that the petitioner can
be granted anticipatory bail. We order that in the event of arrest
of the petitioner in connection with the offence enumerated above,
he shall be released on bail, subject to such terms and conditions
that the Investigating Officer (for short “I.O.”) may deem fit to
impose,  on  condition  also  of  continued  cooperation  in  the
investigation.
6. With the aforesaid, this petition stands disposed of.
7. Pending application(s), if any, also stand disposed of.
 (VISHAL ANAND)                                    (POOJA SHARMA)
DEPUTY REGISTRAR                                 COURT MASTER (NSH)
